title: Anger (Shabbat 105b)
hook: the Talmud likens anger to idol worship

segments.voice: Yesterday: speak good. Did the sentence you found reach someone's ears? Today, a turn from speech to the traits underneath it. First, the hottest one. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-six.

A cupboard door slammed hard enough to bounce back open. A phone thrown onto the couch. A plate set down a little too loudly, and everyone at the table goes quiet. Sometimes anger reaches the hands before it reaches the words. A page of the Talmud lists exactly that kind of moment: tearing your clothes, breaking your dishes, flinging your money. And then it reaches for a startling comparison. Today's word is the thing doing the throwing.
screen: `A DOOR SLAMMED, A PLATE DROPPED.` → `SOMETIMES THE HANDS GO FIRST.` → `A STARTLING COMPARISON.`

segments.voice: Ka'as. Anger. Turn it four ways. First, the passage. In tractate Shabbat, the Talmud says that one who tears his garments in anger, breaks his vessels in anger, or scatters his money in anger should be seen as one who worships idols. Idolatry, in Jewish thought, is a grave charge. So why would a smashed plate earn it? Second, the reason the Talmud gives. That's how the evil inclination works, it says: today it tells you, do this; tomorrow it tells you, do that; until it tells you, go worship idols, and you go. Anger is practice in obeying a voice that isn't yours. Each small surrender trains the next, bigger one. Third, the verse behind it. A psalm says: "There shall no strange god be in thee." The rabbis in the same passage ask what strange god could live inside a person's body, and they answer: the evil inclination. Read that way, the idol isn't a statue in a faraway temple. It's whatever takes the throne inside you for the length of a rage. In that moment, something else is in charge, and you are doing what it says. Fourth, the ordinary Tuesday version. Pirkei Avot has a short line, from Rabbi Eliezer: don't be quick to anger. Not never angry. Slow. Mussar teachers build on that: the space between feeling the heat and acting on it is where a person gets to decide who sits on the throne. Anger may be justified. The tradition's worry is the moment it starts giving the orders. A breath before the door slams is a small act of loyalty to who you mean to be.
screen: `CLOTHES, DISHES, MONEY, IN ANGER.` · `TODAY THIS, TOMORROW IDOLS.` · `NO STRANGE GOD IN THEE.` · `NOT NEVER ANGRY. SLOW.` · then, large: `ANGER IS IDOLATRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cool one anger before it speaks. Settle, and breathe. Bring up something that has made you angry lately. Not the biggest thing; something mid-sized. Let a little of the heat come back. Notice where it lives: jaw, chest, hands. Now notice the words it wants to say, the message it wants to send. Don't send them. Just watch the anger the way you'd watch weather from a window. Breathe slowly, and ask: if I answered this tomorrow instead of today, what would I say? Let that calmer sentence form. If you pray, you can ask in your own words to be slow to anger. The bell holds the time.
Ka'as. Anger. The Talmud compares acting out in anger to serving a strange god, because for that moment, something else is in command. Today's word.
Your line: anger is idolatry. Today, when the heat rises, put one full breath between the feeling and your hands, and another before the words. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Jews study the Talmud's teaching in Shabbat 105b and Avot's counsel to be slow to anger; Mussar groups often take anger as a trait to work on, practicing a pause before reacting.

myth: the Talmud says any feeling of anger is idolatry
it names acting out: tearing clothes, breaking dishes, flinging money in anger.
the Talmud explains it by the evil inclination's habits
today it says do this, tomorrow do that, until it says worship idols.
Avot says never to be angry
Rabbi Eliezer's line is don't be quick to anger: slow, not never.

fork.setup: someone wrecks your plans and you want to throw your phone across the room. according to Shabbat 105b, why does it matter?
options: because each surrender trains you to obey a voice not your own.
fork.reveal: the Talmud says the evil inclination works step by step: today this, tomorrow that, until it says worship idols.

original.note: Hebrew: anger, vexation; the word the Talmud uses in Shabbat 105b.

trapdoor: what you thought: anger is just a bad mood.
what it means: in anger, something else takes command, and acting it out is serving it.
what a scholar hears: Shabbat 105b links the 'strange god' of Psalm 81 to the inclination within, so idolatry becomes an inner throne, not only a statue.

sources.quoted: There shall no strange god be in thee

notes: Shabbat 105b paraphrased: tearing garments, breaking vessels, scattering money in anger 'should be in your eyes like an idol worshipper', and the evil inclination's 'today do this, tomorrow do that' progression; the 'strange god in the body' reading of Psalm 81:10 appears in the same passage. Confirm.
Psalm 81:10 is the JPS 1917 numbering (KJV 81:9); confirm wording.
Avot 2:10 (Rabbi Eliezer: 'do not be easily angered'; numbering varies, 2:10 or 2:15) paraphrased. Confirm.
'Idolatry is about as serious a charge as exists' is a general characterization, not a count; confirm acceptable.
